shards.title: RAII makes cleanup follow object lifetime
shards.content:
Resource Acquisition Is Initialization binds cleanup to an owning object's destructor. Scope exit and exception unwinding then release resources automatically.

Caveat: RAII handles cleanup, not rollback of every change an operation makes.
shards.prompt: What responsibility does an RAII object's destructor carry?

shards.title: Storage and object lifetime are different
shards.content:
An object's lifetime usually begins when suitable storage exists and initialization finishes. For a class object, its lifetime ends when the destructor starts. Having an address does not prove that a live object remains there.

Caveat: construction, destruction, unions, and reused storage have additional rules. Treat this as the ordinary-object model, not a replacement for those rules.
shards.prompt: What must be true besides having allocated storage before you can use an object normally?

shards.title: Ownership names who must release a resource
shards.content:
Ownership is responsibility for release. Make it visible in types such as `std::unique_ptr`. Treat raw pointers and references as borrowed access in new code.

Caveat: that borrowing convention is guidance, not a language guarantee for legacy pointers.
shards.prompt: What question does ownership answer that a raw address does not?

shards.title: unique_ptr transfers ownership without copying it
shards.prompt: After moving a unique_ptr into another unique_ptr, who owns the object and what is the source pointer's state?

shards.title: std::move enables an operation to move
shards.prompt: Which line actually performs a string move, and why does std::move alone not empty the string?

shards.title: A const reference restricts an access path
shards.prompt: Why can a value observed through a const reference change?

shards.title: Vector reallocation breaks borrowed element access
shards.prompt: Why does keeping the vector alive not guarantee that a reference to one of its old elements stays valid?

shards.title: Undefined behavior removes the language's guarantees
shards.prompt: Why is a test run that happens to work insufficient evidence that undefined behavior is safe?

shards.title: Cleanup and rollback are different guarantees
shards.content:
Exception safety describes the state left after failure. The basic guarantee preserves valid state without leaks. The strong guarantee also leaves the observable state unchanged. A no-throw guarantee prevents exceptions from escaping.

Caveat: RAII supports cleanup, but rollback needs deliberate design.
shards.prompt: What does the strong exception guarantee add beyond the basic guarantee?

shards.title: An invariant makes a class safe to use
shards.content:
An invariant is a condition that valid objects maintain, such as a range's `lower <= upper`. Constructors establish it and public operations preserve it.

Caveat: private fields help control updates, but access control alone cannot make an invariant true.
shards.prompt: What must a constructor and a mutating operation do to protect a class invariant?

shards.title: A method body can use a later-declared nested type
shards.prompt: Why does Later work inside read's body, while an earlier return type using Later needs separate care?

shards.title: Common mistake: a reference keeps its object alive
shards.prompt: After owner.reset(), why is reading borrowed invalid even though borrowed is still in scope?

unique_ptr uses destruction to invoke its owned object's deleter.
The pointer type expresses exclusive ownership.

Move operations can transfer ownership, but the cast alone does not.
A borrowed read-only access path does not carry release responsibility.
A reference must still refer to an object whose lifetime permits access.
The container can remain alive after the referenced old elements are gone.
Reading through invalidated element references can violate object lifetime rules.
Automatic cleanup supports leak prevention during failure.
Objects that survive an operation's failure must still be valid.
Resource ownership can be part of a class's valid-state conditions.
The mistaken model assigns ownership to a borrowed reference.
A live reference can name an object whose lifetime has already ended.
Resetting the owner destroys the object, despite outstanding references.
Reading the destroyed int through the dangling reference is invalid.
